description: Sanskrit-into-English songcraft exhibits for L4 work. Each entry names the device used and what it cost. Query by meter, device, rasa, or translator. Entries with sanskrit_iast null are translation-pair exhibits (verse text not captured); the exhibit is the English comparison.

english: With body worn as thine, with pain as deep,
With tears and ceaseless longings answering thine,
With sighs more burning than the sighs that keep
Thy lips ascorch -- doomed far from thee to pine,
He too doth weave the fancies that thy soul entwine.
entries.license_cost: High: rhyme-engine replaces repetition-engine (reads beautifully); sanitizes body-union ('weave the fancies' for 'with his body he enters'); Westernized diction ('doth'). The canonical rhyme-twist warning (mistakes.md #17).
entries.sanskrit_iast: aṅgenāṅgaṃ tanu ca tanunā gāḍhataptena taptaṃ / sāsreṇāsradravam aviratotkaṇṭham utkaṇṭhitena / uṣṇocchvāsaṃ samadhikatarocchvāsinā dūravartī / saṃkalpais te viśati vidhinā vairiṇā ruddhamārgaḥ
entries.source: Arthur W. Ryder, The Cloud-Messenger (1912); via complete-review.com + textetc workshop

english: With his body thy body he enters; all-haggard body with haggard;
Fevered with intensely fevered; tear-flowing with tearful; incessantly eager
With eager; hotly sighing with yet more abundantly sighing;
In his thoughts, far distant as he is, and the way barred by adverse fate.
entries.license_cost: None on doctrine; high on music — reads as legal circumlocution. The pole opposite Ryder: all transmission, no song.
entries.source: Franklin & Eleanor Edgerton translation; via complete-review.com

english: 'He, far off, a hostile fate blocking
his way, by mere wish joins his body
with your body, his thinness with your thinness,
his pain with your intense pain, his tears
with your tears, his endless longing
with your longing, his deep sigh with your sigh.'
entries.license_cost: Low: keeps every pair, loses the Sanskrit's knotted simultaneity. The middle path — closest to what L2 already does; L4 must go further into music.
entries.source: Leonard Nathan, The Transport of Love (1976); via complete-review.com

english: The sun, his horses with bent necks,
with plumes striking on their eyes,
goes home, yoke riding high upon their manes,
setting the day to rest in ocean.
entries.license_cost: None visible: miniature strokes fitted into one grammatical frame; line-final diphthongs sinking to deep 'au' mirror the sun sinking. Vowel music is free.
entries.sanskrit_iast: so 'yam ānataśirodharair hayaiḥ / karṇacāmaravighaṭṭitekṣaṇaiḥ / astam eti yugabhugnakesaraiḥ / saṃnidhāya divasaṃ mahodadhau
entries.source: Ingalls, An Anthology of Sanskrit Court Poetry intro (HOS 44, 1965); via IIT-K excerpts

english: You could pick up the drops of moonlight shaken off by the leaves and scattered like flowers on the ground beneath the branches, and deck your hair with them.
LITERAL: It is possible, if by your fingers plucked, with these soft under-the-branches-fallen-flowers, these leaf-shaken moonbeam drops, to deck your hair.
entries.form: song line + deliberately unintelligible literal (method exhibit)
entries.license_cost: Exhibit of method, not a reading text: proves our stack already owns this split (L2 = the diamond, L4 = the song). Never compress both jobs into one layer.
entries.sanskrit_note: verse text not captured; exhibit is the translation pair
entries.source: Ingalls, An Anthology of Sanskrit Court Poetry intro (HOS 44, 1965)

english: Her breasts are brother kings, equal in nobility, reared together till they have reached the same altitude of fame; and from their border warfare these monarchs of vast provinces have gained a cursed hardness.
entries.license_cost: Low: every term kept (kings, nobility, heights, provinces, battles, hardness); music in joints (word order, cadence).
entries.sanskrit_note: verse text not captured; exhibit is the same-verse trio
entries.source: Ingalls trans.; via Wikipedia Bhavakadevi (citing Octavio Paz, In Light of India)

english: Her breasts are two brother kings, equal in nobility, looking out from the same heights, side by side, sovereigns of the vast provinces they have won in frontier battles, with a defiant hardness.
entries.license_cost: Low: same fidelity as Ingalls, different music (parataxis vs period). Proof that cadence is the cheapest safest instrument.
entries.source: Octavio Paz, In Light of India; via Wikipedia Bhavakadevi

english: Clouds thicken the sky.
Tamala trees darken the forest.
The night frightens him.
Radha, you take him home!
They leave at Nanda's order,
Passing trees in thickets on the way,
Until secret passions of Radha and Madhava
Triumph on the Jumna riverbank.
entries.license_cost: Medium: celebrated translation; Holcombe critique — lines are 'self-contained prose units, marked by occasional alliteration but not cadenced'; English lacks means to harmonize the Sanskrit measures, result can be cacophony. Ambiguity of voices flattened (Nanda/Radha/Krishna composite).
entries.sanskrit_iast: meghair meduram ambaraṃ vanabhuvaḥ śyāmās tamāladrumair / naktaṃ bhīrur ayaṃ tvam eva tad imāṃ rādhe gṛhaṃ prāpaya
entries.source: Barbara Stoler Miller, Love Song of the Dark Lord (Columbia, 1977); via archive.org full text + IIT-K excerpts

english: Look to Hari in the spring,
dancing with his youthful women:
how endlessly the pain encircles
one who's solitary, my friend.
entries.license_cost: Low: assonance stands in for yamaka (never rhyme); octosyllabic line carries dance-energy; pentameter reserved for narrative sections. The refrain method L4 adopts.
entries.rasa: vipralambha-srngara (spring as cruelty to the separated)
entries.sanskrit_iast: harir iha mugdhavadhūnikare vilāsinī vilasati kelipare
entries.source: C. John Holcombe, textetc Gitagovinda workshop (wt-jayadeva-1) vs Miller/Siegel/Rao

english: Flame-flower crimson Ashóka-tree, where has she gone?
Why left she this heart aflame?
entries.license_cost: High effort, partial success — Brough: 'Only on very rare occasions can we hope to imitate at all closely in translation any of the Sanskrit metres.' Method viable only for short regular meters.
entries.sanskrit_iast: raktāśoka kṛśodari kva nu gatā tyaktvānuraktaṃ janaṃ / no dṛṣṭeti mudhaiva cālayasi yad vātābhibhūtaṃ śiraḥ
entries.source: John Brough, Poems from the Sanskrit (1968) intro; via Pokharel 2025

english: Ever for you is my love, ever constant, kind.
Never unfaithful: a heart ever true I gave.
Tell me, my darling - forgiveness I pray to find-
Where is the fault that you found in your humble slave?
entries.license_cost: Low: Brough's one clean success — works because the meter is short and regular enough for stress to stand in for quantity. Sanction for imitating ONLY short regular meters, if ever.
entries.sanskrit_iast: tvayi nibaddharateḥ priyavādinaḥ / praṇayabhaṅgaparāṅmukhacetasaḥ / kam aparādhalavam mama paśyasi / tyajasi mānini dāsajanaṃ yataḥ
entries.source: John Brough, Poems from the Sanskrit (1968); Kalidasa Vikramorvasiya excerpt; via Pokharel 2025

english: She is God's vision, of pure thought
Composed in His creative mind.
entries.license_cost: Low-medium: Anglicized (loses Indian-Sanskrit aspects per complete-review) but stage-alive (Berkeley 1907 Greek Theatre). The speakability test L4 adopts: if the actor can't breathe it, rescore it.
entries.sanskrit_note: verse text not captured; exhibit is the stage-song method
entries.source: Arthur W. Ryder, Translations of Shakuntala and Other Works (1912); staged Berkeley 1907

entries.english_after: In the heart, Kāma wakes to kill.
entries.english_before: Kāma arises in the heart, to kill.
entries.license_cost: None: same ids, faster gait. 'wakes' sudden alive; 7 words = the violence of the arising.
entries.rasa: srngara turning to vira (violence of desire in tenderness)
entries.rasa_reason: wakes > arises (more sudden, more alive); brevity (7 words) = the violence of the arising
entries.sanskrit_note: translation-work own L2 craft; Sanskrit in ghatakarpara data
entries.source: translation-work ghatakarpara pass; EXAMPLES.md rasa table

entries.license_cost: None: dash sets the absence apart as a presence.
entries.rasa_reason: em-dash isolates 'the separated beloved' — the absence becomes a presence, set apart
entries.source: translation-work ghatakarpara pass; EXAMPLES.md rasa table

entries.english_after: By that cruel one who serves a foreign land, you will kill me — without him.
entries.english_before: By the cruel one serving a foreign land, you will kill me without him.
entries.license_cost: None: 'that' points (particularizes = anti-sadharanikarana where the Sanskrit points); dash isolates the ache.
entries.rasa_reason: 'that cruel one' > 'the cruel one' (more pointed); em-dash isolates 'without him' — the ache
entries.source: translation-work ghatakarpara pass; EXAMPLES.md rasa table

entries.english_after: Release your foreign love today — or your wife: what more is there to say?
entries.english_before: Release foreign-land love today, or your wife — what is to be said?
entries.license_cost: None: colon creates the ultimatum; closing question carries exasperation.
entries.rasa_reason: colon creates the ultimatum; 'what more is there to say?' carries the exasperation
entries.source: translation-work ghatakarpara pass; EXAMPLES.md rasa table

entries.english_after: The cātaka, gasping, begs for rain — and nothing else.
entries.license_cost: None: 'rain' is lore-exact (cātaka drinks only rain); coda carries singularity of thirst.
entries.rasa_reason: gasping > thirsty (desperation); rain > water (cātaka drinks only rain); 'and nothing else' carries the singularity
entries.source: translation-work ghatakarpara pass; EXAMPLES.md rasa table

entries.english_after: The suffering traveler — she is your beloved.
entries.english_before: The suffering traveler, she is your beloved.
entries.license_cost: None: dash creates the identification.
entries.rasa_reason: dash creates the identification: the traveler IS the beloved
entries.source: translation-work ghatakarpara pass; EXAMPLES.md rasa table

entries.english_after: Drowned in sorrow-ocean's water; remembrance of your virtue alone keeps her afloat.
entries.english_before: Fallen into sorrow-ocean's water; remembrance of your virtue alone protects her.
entries.license_cost: None: same doctrine, wetter words.
entries.rasa_reason: drowned > fallen (more violent); keeps her afloat > protects (more visceral)
entries.source: translation-work ghatakarpara pass; EXAMPLES.md rasa table

entries.english_after: Your flower-looked-at body — I would release it quickly, nīpa, body.
entries.english_before: Your flower-looked-at body, I would release, quickly, nīpa, body.
entries.license_cost: None: compound ambiguity preserved (flower-looked-at body vs body-looked-at-by-flowers both live); dash is the surrender-pause.
entries.rasa_reason: dash creates the pause of surrender before the release; English preserves the compound's ambiguity (BOUNDARY in C1)

entries.english_before: Loud roar, water in caves falls, wonderful-formed beauties.
